title: The Bottle
subtitle: The Carroll A. Deering · Cape Hatteras, 1921
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the stormy winter coast of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, in early 1921, grey heavy overcast, cold slate-blue sea and white surf, weathered wood, old glass and salt-stained paper of the early 1920s, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. April nineteen twenty-one. A fisherman handed in a bottle. Inside, a note about a ghost ship.
beats.img: A single old green glass bottle with a cork, a rolled paper note visible inside it, lying on wet dark sand at the edge of the surf, centred and large in frame, sharply lit by soft grey daylight, thin foam around it, the grey winter sea blurred behind. No writing visible.

beats.vo: Ten weeks earlier, the schooner Carroll A. Deering had been found aground offshore, sails still set. Her crew was gone.
beats.img: A five-masted wooden schooner from the early 1920s stranded on an offshore sandbar, sails set and slack, white surf breaking around the hull, seen from mid-distance, centred in frame, grey winter Atlantic under low overcast, deserted and eerie.

beats.vo: The note said the Deering had been captured by another boat, and asked whoever found it to send word.
beats.img: A small torn scrap of old paper with faint smudged pencil marks that cannot be read, lying unrolled on a weathered wooden table beside an uncorked glass bottle, a dim oil lamp glow, cold grey window light, quiet and close.

beats.vo: Five federal departments investigated. Handwriting experts concluded the note was forged.
beats.img: A plain government office desk in the early 1920s, a magnifying glass resting on a small scrap of paper beside an empty glass bottle, a green-shaded desk lamp, filing cabinets in shadow, grey winter daylight from a tall window, no people.

beats.vo: The fisherman admitted he wrote it himself, hoping for a job at the lighthouse. The real crew was never found.
beats.img: A tall coastal lighthouse tower standing alone on a low windswept sand shore at dusk, centred in frame, its light faint against a heavy grey storm sky, dune grass bent by wind, rough grey sea beyond, lonely.

facts.claim: In April 1921 (April 11) a local Buxton (Cape Hatteras area) fisherman, Christopher Columbus Gray, reported finding a bottle containing a note about the Deering and turned it over to authorities
The Deering has been called the 'Ghost Ship' of the Outer Banks
The Carroll A. Deering, a five-masted schooner, was found aground on Diamond Shoals off Cape Hatteras on January 31, 1921 (about ten weeks before April 11) with sails set
The crew was gone; no sign of them aboard
The note claimed the Deering had been captured by an 'oil burning boat' and asked the finder to notify the Deering's headquarters
Five federal departments (Commerce, Treasury, Justice, Navy, State) investigated
Federal handwriting experts (Treasury, Navy) concluded the note was forged / a hoax
The fisherman confessed he forged the note himself
His motive: he hoped the publicity would help him get a job at the Cape Hatteras light station

The crew was never found; the case remains unsolved (yacht.de April 2026: dropped end of 1922 without final conclusion; National Archives Hoover blog: unsolved to this day; USCG: never been solved). No 2024-2026 resolution found.
